SOAP Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaints: 3-day history of watery diarrhoea with urgency, central lower abdominal pain, and one episode of vomiting this morning; associated mild nausea. No visible blood in stool or vomitus. No chest pain. Baseline asthma symptoms only.
- Symptom course: Neither improving nor worsening over 3 days. Pain partially relieved after bowel motions. Frequency of stools prevents work attendance. Feels inadequately hydrated. No documented fever though reports mild sweating over the last 4 days.
- Past medical history: Asthma.
- Medications: Inhaler for asthma (brand/dose/route/frequency not documented; recently changed to a new inhaler purchased locally).
- Social history: Employed; currently staying home due to symptoms. Further details not elicited.
- Allergies: NKDA.
- Family history (relevant): Father died of bowel (colorectal) cancer 10 years ago.

Objective:
- No vital signs or clinician-performed physical examination available (tele-consult).
- Patient-reported finding: Mild tenderness on self-palpation of mid-abdomen.
- No investigations performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute diarrhoea with abdominal pain
   - Assessment: Suspected viral or food-borne gastroenteritis.
   - Differential diagnosis: Less likely inflammatory bowel disease, medication-related reaction, early presentation of colorectal pathology (family history).
   - Investigations planned: None at present; advise in-person review and stool studies if symptoms persist >48 h or worsen.
   - Treatment planned: Oral rehydration—encourage adequate fluid intake; dietary rest as tolerated. Avoid antibiotics unless clinically indicated.
   - Safety-net advice: Monitor for fever, bloody stool/vomit, increasing pain, or signs of dehydration; attend GP/urgent care if any occur.

2. Risk assessment given family history of colorectal cancer
   - Assessment: Current presentation not suggestive of malignancy; however, positive family history noted.
   - Investigations planned: Discuss routine colorectal cancer screening with GP once acute illness resolved.
   - Relevant referrals: GP for future screening discussion.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Accurate vitals, full physical exam, medication list with doses/frequencies, smoking/alcohol status.  
● Internal conflicts: DOB stated as “1 Jan 1992” yet patient later says age 48 (implies ~1972); conflict noted. Patient initially unsure about blood in vomit, later denies.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional inaudible/fragmented phrases but clinical content understandable.
